description: I'm Will Medina, a software engineer and product designer in Denver, originally from Lima, Peru. I started coding websites at 11 and never stopped. Over 10+ years, human-computer interaction became my favorite part of the work: making software that people understand at a glance. Moon exploration fascinates me, and I'm here to build a clear tool for a hard call.
summary:
Nanta is a web app for exploring space, a step at a time. You start the journey in the solar system and navigate bodies like the Moon, Earth, Mars or Mercury. As you choose a body and a site, the camera flies you to it, landing on the location's horizon. There you can pick or create windows of dates, and Nanta shows where the Sun and the Earth are from that spot, alongside JPL Horizons data and imagery of the ground.

I approached it as a study, and everything came back to the horizon. At the south pole one degree of Sun decides power, so I drew the horizon as a compass from the site. I designed from the user's side with one stable screen, common interactions, and standards like WCAG and NASA-STD-3001. Plans move, so sites and dates stay separate and Nanta compares them like a diff, so a launch slip or a moved landing reads as a change. The URL holds the state, so a shared link opens the same view.

Growing up in Peru, I wondered how the Inca studied the sky before telescopes. That wonder drew me to space, so I gave the project a Quechua name. Nanta means "the path you choose."
details:
Nanta is Quechua for "the path you choose." Growing up in Peru, I wondered how the Inca studied the sky before telescopes, watching the Sun so closely that they built gates and roads around it. That curiosity first drew me to space, and the name connects where I come from with aerospace. Picking a landing site is that same kind of choice.

How it works

Nanta opens on the solar system as it is right now, placed from JPL Horizons. You choose a body and the camera flies to it, then a site and you land on its horizon. Pick or create a window of dates, and Nanta shows where the Sun and the Earth are from that spot, every hour. A compass draws the horizon from above so one degree is easy to see, next to the hours of sunlight and Earth in view, the time to the next sunset or Earthset, and the raw numbers. A time slider moves everything together, and imagery shows the ground.

Benefits

It helps when plans change. Sites and dates are separate, so a launch slip or a moved landing is one change away. You pin pairs as candidates and compare them like a diff, green for more of a condition and red for less. Nanta never scores a site, it shows the numbers and leaves the decision to people. The URL holds the state, so a shared link opens the same view.

Impact

The goal is to bring this data to mission planners, educators and the public on one screen, and to make space feel a little closer.

Architecture

I decided not to build my own data service or database. Nanta reads straight from NASA's APIs through thin wrappers on Cloudflare Workers, which shape each answer for the screen and cache it at the edge. Your own sites, windows and candidates stay in your browser. This keeps it light and makes it easy to plug in more sources later.

Tech stack

  • TypeScript, React 19 rendered on the server and resumed in the browser
  • Three.js for the 3D model
  • Tailwind CSS, esbuild, Biome, and Node's test runner
  • Cloudflare Workers for hosting and edge caching
  • JPL Horizons for positions
  • Moon Trek, Mars Trek and Mercury Trek for imagery
  • GIBS for Earth imagery, Blue Marble and NOAA-20 VIIRS
  • Claude Code to assist with code and checks
  • Three runtime dependencies (React, React DOM and Three.js)

Creativity

Site selection works as exploration, not a form, and the comparison borrows from games and git diffs, things people already know how to read. The design draws on Andean culture, with cochineal red, the dye of Inca textiles, as the accent.

Considerations

I put accuracy first, with the model checked against Horizons within a few tenths of a degree. The interface follows WCAG and ARIA practices, and uses NASA-STD-3001 as a guide for contrast and legibility, though some areas of it still need more validation, ideally on real displays with real operators.

What's next

There was a lot for me to learn along the way, and some parts took longer than I expected. I chose to focus on the experience and on keeping it easy to use, so some features, like terrain from LOLA heights, are still ahead.
